summary.text: Case 1: a neonate with a giant sacrococcygeal mass seen on prenatal ultrasound (two months before birth); the mother had vaginal bleeding and complete anterior placenta previa, and received dexamethasone and magnesium sulfate before cesarean section. The newborn presented with weak spontaneous respiration and hypotonia at birth and was intubated and resuscitated (Apgar 8, 9, 9).

CT showed a large predominantly cystic pelvic-floor mass approximately 24.0 x 16.9 x 17.5 cm with solid edge components and punctate calcifications. Resection was done on the first day after birth with coccyx tip resection and complete excision; pathology showed giant mature teratoma. AFP was >3,000.0 µg/L before surgery and 17 days after, and 3.5 µg/L 1 year later.

A rectal examination found a palpable cystic mass (about 3.0 x 4.0 cm) and MRI showed a cystic lesion; MRI 1.5 years after surgery showed slight shrinkage and a second surgery completed the excision (cystic mature teratoma, no immature components). Pelvic MRI 2 years after the second surgery showed the cystic lesion essentially disappeared.

summary.text: Case 2: a neonate born at a gestational age of 32 weeks and 6 days, birth weight 3,680 g, with a sacrococcygeal mass of approximately 20 x 16 x 11 cm and AFP >192,000.0 µg/L; MRI showed a large cystic-solid mass extending into the pelvis. Resection with partial coccygectomy and drainage was performed on the second day after birth.

Significant intraoperative wound bleeding (estimated blood loss about 300 mL) was managed with red cell suspension and plasma transfusion; a small amount of persistent wound bleeding was seen on the first postoperative day. Laboratory tests showed PT 20.3 s, PT-INR 1.78, APTT 64.9 s, fibrinogen 1.03 g/L and HGB 119 g/L, and washed red cells, platelets and plasma were subsequently transfused. Pathology showed immature teratoma, grade 3; AFP gradually decreased postoperatively and ultrasound at 4 months postoperatively showed no abnormalities.
